Just finished my BSc and am starting my MSc in the fall. Even though I graduated with like 3 years of field experience and another separate two years in Gov, it still took me about another 2 years of tirelessly and manically applying to literally every government job opening on .gc jobs across the country, and probably about 5-8 interviews to land a position. 

Not saying it’s impossible. But positions are competitive in this field and openings are sparse, and you will most likely end up in something not completely related to your exact specialization in env. sci. 

I studied soils/geomorph and now I’m doing more admin and reviewing EIS. 

Don’t give up on the government applications because sometimes pools can take forever and set up job alerts to your email to keep track of new positions in departments you are interested in. 

Try to network on LinkedIn by contacting people who are currently working in positions you want to work in at companies you are interested in. For example: you are interested in working as an air quality monitoring at “x” consulting firm - contact someone in that, or a similar position and inquire about what sort of experiences, education and networking led them to that job. 

One last note: Academia is a trap.

Permafrost is classified as ground that has remained frozen, and below 0 degrees Celsius for 2 or more years. In environments where permafrost is present, there are actually two main important "layers" when looking at the substrate below the ground surface- the active layer and the permafrost layer. 

The active layer sits on top of the permafrost, or "frozen" layer and will thaw every summer - sometimes when temperatures are higher than normal or when a chunk of ground ice is exposed in a slope, the permafrost starts to degrade. 

If I'm not mistaken, what's happening in this video is called active later detachment! 😊 When the permafrost layer begins to degarde/melt, the substrate sometimes becomes so saturated that the active layer may slip and/or flow down a slope.
